title: Your A-share losses come from understanding that can't keep pace with change
dek: After reviewing his 60+-percent drawdown this year, Zhang Jun discovered that the root cause of A-shares' short bull runs and long bear markets—and investors' short time horizons—was never the market itself, but investors' understanding of intrinsic value and macroeconomic cycles failing to keep pace with change's speed.
why: An honest retrospective from a fund manager running private equity for years after a major drawdown, from rereading Graham's original work to the storage-chip case—information-dense.
who: Individual investors managing stock portfolios, fund managers, and anyone seeking to understand value investing's underlying logic rather than mechanically copying formulas.
skip: 1:04–1:20, philosophical discussion on learning the I Ching, reading notes, and life's meaning—personal reflection only—can be skipped.

points.h: The index barely moved, but whole sectors were sliced in half
points.body: Zhang Jun highlights a counterintuitive fact: Shanghai Composite's full-year range was under 20 percent, from January highs above 4,200 to lows above 3,600. Yet beneath that, sub-indices swung wildly. ChiNext and STAR Board each fell roughly 40 percent from June peaks; the optical module index dropped over 50 percent from its high. His point: concentrated sector bets faced far steeper drawdowns than the aggregate index suggests.

points.h: Even dividend low-volatility funds got turned into high-volatility assets
points.body: Zhang Jun adds that supposedly defensive dividend plays didn't escape the carnage: the baijiu index fell 30-odd percent on its worst days; the dividend low-volatility index—promised stability—was down 10 points in its worst month. More tragicomically, in June when the market rallied and tech soared, this index fell 10 points in a single month, then gained them back in July when the market fell—behaving the exact opposite of its name.

points.h: Every industry has its own Xu Jiayin
points.body: Zhang Jun argues Chinese firms cannot sustain stable EPS growth because of abundant ‘entrepreneurial ambition’: CEOs want to expand scale, CFOs and key technologists push expansion and capex to advance their careers, and local governments' investment drives force companies to boost capital spending. Everyone knows Xu Jiayin, he notes, but every industry has its own version—the property sector's just leveraged hard enough to crater publicly.

points.h: Graham never said to discount future cash flows
points.body: Zhang Jun revisits years of misreading Graham: value investors picture DCF models calculating intrinsic value, but that was Williams' idea, not Graham's. In “Security Analysis”, Graham calculated working capital and net asset discounts—the goal was finding a margin of safety, not pinning an exact intrinsic value number. He restates Graham's actual logic in three sentences: stocks are stakes in businesses; Mr. Market is a quotation device to exploit; and margins of safety matter.

points.h: Intrinsic value isn't a point—it's a moving range
points.body: He cites a cutting-tool stock he sold too early this year: bought at 2 billion+ market cap aiming for 10 billion in three years, but AI-driven M&A turbocharged earnings to target, so he sold per plan—only later discovering the company's intrinsic value was still climbing fast and he'd treated a dynamic company as static. Takeaway: intrinsic value is never a fixed point but a range that shifts up and down with fundamentals; exit timing should track that range's velocity.

points.h: Storage chip prices spike, but intrinsic value may not follow
points.body: When asked whether ‘rising demand equals rising intrinsic value,’ Zhang Jun uses storage chips to refute the simple narrative: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron learned overexpansion's sting, intentionally restrained supply to barely maintain a three-player oligopoly—then AI sent prices skyward, but now they're expanding again while YMTC enters. His conclusion: once a carefully guarded competitive structure cracks, surface price rallies and demand figures don't simply equal long-term intrinsic-value gains.

points.h: Whether to add on dips—the question itself is the answer
points.body: Facing scenarios where stock price falls below your entry but intrinsic value falls faster (so margin of safety looks bigger), Zhang Jun offers this heuristic: if you're asking friends whether to add to a losing position, that act alone proves you don't understand it well enough—sell immediately. As long as intrinsic value is still sliding and you can't find new evidence of a bottom, buying purely because the price is low is short-term gambling and probably catching a knife mid-fall.

points.h: Value investors with sweeping sector coverage—I'm skeptical
points.body: Zhang Jun offers an ‘immature observation’: no one can be expert in packaged food, consumer electronics, and AI simultaneously. If someone calling themselves a value investor covers too many industries, he doubts their authenticity. He reviews his own past expansion into chemicals, pharma, information security, and solar—convinced at the time he was applying value-investing method, but in hindsight nearly every call was wrong. Example: pharma volume-based pricing policy disruptions happened long before he grasped that industry logic had shifted.

points.h: Effort breeds error; comfort invites crisis
points.body: Zhang Jun distills two mental models from this year's repeated mistakes: ‘effort breeds error’—the moment you deliberately strain to forecast or trade, bias enters; ‘comfort invites crisis’—the moment you think ‘good enough, time to rest,’ danger usually arrives. He cites late February as proof: market rallied to his year-start target and he was unwinding when an unexpected headline triggered another crash, proving the pattern once more.

quotes.text: This index dropped 10 points in a single month—that's how the market turned dividend low-volatility into dividend high-volatility.
There are two mistakes: one is adding at the peak, the other is selling at the bottom. Just avoid these two.
Graham's actual words are these three sentences: First, buying stocks is buying a company. Second, Mr. Market is here to give you a quote.
But we need to understand that intrinsic value isn't a single point—it's a range, and this range moves up or down.
You ask, so what should I do? Should I buy? Add more? Or sell? If David and I are really close friends, I'd tell him: the fact that you're asking me this means you're uncertain.

You can't claim to be expert in packaged food, consumer electronics, and AI all at once—that's overreaching. So I'll offer an immature observation: if a value investor covers too many industries, I doubt whether he's genuinely a value investor.
The first principle is ‘effort breeds error’—the moment you strain, bias creeps in. The second is ‘comfort invites crisis’—you think ‘good enough, everything's fine’—and then it hits.
So our problem is always this: insufficient self-knowledge leads to insufficient understanding of the macro economy and the market.
